Q: Database design for high-frequency options tick data (fast ingestion + query performance) A:

I've little experience with working on stocks/trading/options both personally and professionally. Expect this part, I've had many use cases in past to handle huge data ingestion workloads. For those usecases there were two different solution that I developed depending on how much operational overhead we could handle and whether we had proper infrastructure or not. Mind it these are my experience in developing those solutions, you will have to tweak them to you usecases.

E2E aws solution. In this we got the data into S3 buckets as parquet files, ensured schema with aws glue scemas. Used aws athena for queries. For our usecases partitioning data on year, month, day, hour was more than sufficient. This usecase scalled really well for our write heavy usecase. We used aws athena to query data. This worked well for us because our write load was predictable and read usecases involved created daily reports. Later on we added aws quicksight for dashboarding. This thing was really cost efficient for us and barely costed us much $$ compared to other solutions like Flink and self hosted infra. We were able to get this setup up and running in under few days and that worked like charm. You can find more details here, I documented our experience at the time, which has come in handy multiple times since then.

Other solution that I can suggest you can look into is ClickHouse. I've never personally used ClickHouse in production grade setup long enough to get comfortable with it or understand its working. But I know for fact that ClickHouse can handles billions of rows without breaking a sweat. It is OLAP, so expect good query performance as long as you don't botch up schema design.

Q: How do I know when Python makes an approximation in mathematical calculations? A:

See Handling very large numbers in Python.

Python has a BigNum class for holding 200! and will use it automatically.

Your teacher's statement, though not exactly true here is true in general. Computers have limitations, and it is good to know what they are. Remember that every time you add another integer of data storage, you can store a number that is 2^32 (4 billion +) times larger. It is hard to comprehend how many more numbers that is - but maths gets slower as you add more integers to store the exact value of a very large number.

As an example (what you can store with 1000 bits)

Q: Can a method installed on “String.prototype” update the string value in-place? A:

To make it short:

You can't.

Strings are immutable. Once it is made, a string can never be changed.

You have to set your string to an empty string to "clear" it

var str = "String";
str='';

Note that this won't change the string but sets str to a new Instance of a String, the old one gets garbage collected

It is even shorter then calling a Prototypes method of the Object which would do exactly the same. And you don't have to temper with the native Objects prototypes

Edit - Thx for pointing that out Florian Margaine

If you have many occurences of setting empty Strings and might change your future "definition" of clearing, you could either use a funciton that returns `` or a empty String

function clearString () {
    return ''
}
var str = "Asd"
var str = clearString()

Or simply Set a variable to an empty String

var emptyString = ''
var str = "Asd"
str = emptyString //''

Now if you want to change '' into null or undefined

var emptyString = null

Which would work as well, since primitive data types are being passed as value and not by reference

But i would suggest not modifying an Objects prototype for something like this

Q: The correlation between declarative and imperative programming and the complexity of abstraction in coding A:

The term ﻿“correlation” is certainly misused. Correlation is a statistical concept, nothing else. What do you really mean?

The questionable statement formulated in the first paragraph is obviously not true. Your understanding of the term ﻿“declarative” is certainly incorrect. The distinction between declarative and imperative paradigms has nothing to do with the programming language “level” (low/high). However, this understanding can be blurred by the fact that the declarative paradigm requires a higher abstraction level, so it cannot be implemented at a low level. But this dependency is indirect and is unrelated to the concepts themselves.

Your entire post is based on a totally incorrect understanding of things. I would recommend relearning the basics of programming to gain some understanding.

Q: External client apps that are created in ephemeral orgs can't be packaged A:

To enable packaging of an ECA from a namespace org, two steps are required:

1. You must flip a External Client App Setting via a metadata push. Details on the available settings at External Client App Settings.

Retrieve metadata: sf project retrieve start -m Settings:ExternalClientApp

Set enablePackageEcaOauthFromDevOrg to true in ExternalClientApp.settings-meta.xml

Deploy: sf project deploy start -m Settings:ExternalClientApp

Remove Settings file from your local directory as it does not need to be packaged

2. Update your project-scratch-def.json to include the following:

"settings": {
    "externalClientAppSettings": {
        "enablePackageEcaOauthFromDevOrg": true
    },
    ...
}
